newsitem.title: USA: Ample hydropower boxes in NYMEX electricity prices.
newsitem.headline: Ample hydropower boxes in NYMEX electricity prices.

text.p: Electricity futures on the New York Mercantile Exchange are unlikely to stray far from their current price range until after what looks to be a record spring runoff in the Northwest, traders and analysts said.
"There's no (fresh) fundamental news in the market right now. Everyone is in a wait-and-see mode," said a Houston trader. "I don't see March going one way or the other."

The electricity contracts took a hit in late January, dropping about 10 percent after hydrologists predicted brimming reservoirs and plenty of hydropower this spring after one of the wettest winters in decades on the West Coast.
But the power complex has languished since that drop, with a lack of interest draining trade in both the California-Oregon Border (COB) and Palo Verde (PV) contracts.
Daily PV and COB volumes through Wednesday averaged only 114 and 152 contracts, respectively, about half of their volumes a week ago.

Prices have been napping as well. Over the past two weeks the March COB contract has been stuck between $9.75 and $11.25 per megawatt hour (MWh). March PV was trapped in an even tighter range of $12.25 and $13.75.
Some players blamed the slowdown on the time of year, pointing to the end soon of winter heating demand.
They also said the market has turned more cautious ahead of the torrent of cheap power about to pour out of the mountains into the Northwest's vast hydroelectric system.
"You don't want to buy or sell with all the water and the record amount of snow," said another Houston futures trader.

The Northwest River Forecast Center, based in Portland, Ore., said Monday it expects very high spring runoff at most hydroelectric projects, with flows through some dams nearly double their average for the season.
January-July runoff on the Columbia River at The Dalles dam in Oregon will likely reach 137 percent of average for the period, the agency said.
Faced with so much hydropower this spring, many traders are already shifting their attention to summer deliveries.
"There's nothing going on with the nearby months. They are trading farther and farther out," said the second trader.
Some traders said that if natural gas futures or the cash power market snap out of their own doldrums, they may provide direction for the power contracts.
Extended national forecasts point to generally mild weather for the rest of the month, which would likely dampen energy demand across the U.S.
"Barring any strange weather in March, you could see prices heading lower. There's more than enough hydro out there," said Steve Mabry, director of risk management at Noram Energy Services.
Meanwhile, the nearby futures contracts could drop as much as $2 from current levels, he said.
At 1200 EST Friday, the COB March contract was trading at $10.70 per MWh and PV was trading at $13.25.
